SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

J27, J25, J4 OPPOSITION LANDOWNERS' EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners—Bernareggio Family Partners, Ltd., Robert Bowling, and Wendell “Wendy” & Shirley Fleming (collectively, the “J27 Landowners”)—file, as pro se intervenors, these Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) issued August 20, 2026.

Respectively submitted by:
Paul Grimme										     Bernareggio Family Partners, Ltd.						
109 Dove Tail Ln								                 Georgetown, TX 78628								            Mobile: 214-886-1342								              Email: pjgrimme2@gmail.com

I. INTRODUCTION
The J27 Landowners support the PFD’s recommendation that the Applications be denied because Applicants failed to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary. The notice issue was also material in the PFD, but the Commission’s August 28, 2026 order in Docket No. 59315 has now rejected the PFD’s legal interpretation of Rule 22.52(a)(4). The J27 Landowners therefore address notice only briefly, while preserving the factual history for its relevance to community input and the circumstances of this proceeding.
The J27 Landowners also take exception to the routing choice of route 894 and believe a different routing decision path should have been pursued: first, by avoiding the Central Corridor because of its qualitative and irreversible effects on Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park; second, if the Central Corridor was selected, choosing Route 487 over Route 894 because Route 487 provides the better overall balance of the routing factors.
II. TABLE OF PARTIES
J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners: Bernareggio Family Partners, Ltd.; Robert Bowling; and Wendell “Wendy” & Shirley Fleming.
Position: Support denial of the Applications. If the Commission proceeds to routing, oppose selection of the Central Corridor and, if a Central Corridor route is selected, support Route 487 over Route 894.
III. PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES
A. Adequacy of Application
The J27 Landowners do not take exception to the PFD’s treatment of Application adequacy.
B. Notice (Issues 2-3)
The PFD found that Applicants expanded the study area after the June 2025 public meetings and added approximately 400 miles of route links, bringing approximately 1,400 additional landowners into the class entitled to direct-mail notice of the Application.¹
Those facts remain relevant to the history of this proceeding, even though the Commission has rejected the PFD’s legal conclusion that the later routing changes required another public meeting. The June 2025 meetings were intended to solicit input concerning preliminary route links, potential impacts, and community concerns. Approximately 1,400 landowners whose property later entered the filed routing universe did not participate in those meetings.²
In its August 28, 2026 final order in Docket No. 59315, the Commission held that Rule 22.52(a)(4) requires at least one public meeting before filing when 25 or more persons would be entitled to direct-mail notice, but does not require another meeting when a utility later adds route links or expands the study area. The Commission found Oncor satisfied the rule by holding a public meeting and notifying landowners within 500 feet of the preliminary facilities as they existed when notice was sent.³ The Commission also relied on prior CCN proceedings reaching the same result.⁴
The J27 Landowners do not ask the Commission to disregard that precedent. The point here is narrower: the approximately 1,400 later-affected landowners and the post-meeting expansion of the routing universe remain factual circumstances relevant to community input and the development of the final routing alternatives.⁵
C. Public Input
The J27 Landowners do not take exception to the PFD’s treatment of public input except to emphasize that the later-added route corridors could not have been informed by the views of the landowners brought into the routing universe after the public meetings.
D. Need (Issues 5-7)
The J27 Landowners strongly support the PFD’s recommendation of denial on need. The ALJs identified four independent deficiencies: Applicants did not establish Import Path 2 independently from the broader PBRP; the projected loads underlying the PBRP had changed sufficiently to warrant reevaluation; Applicants did not establish sufficient generation at Bell County East to perform the asserted westbound function; and the record contains credible evidence that new and planned gas generation in the Permian Basin could reduce or eliminate the need for the proposed transmission expansion.⁵
These findings are particularly important because the record is not static. The PFD recognizes changed load assumptions and identifies new gas generation as an alternative that could reduce or eliminate the need for the proposed transmission expansion.⁶ The Commission should adopt the ALJs’ conclusion that Applicants failed to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.⁷
Recent developments reinforce the need for the Commission to exercise caution before approving this Project. On August 28, 2026, Attorney General Ken Paxton filed an amicus brief supporting American Stewards of Liberty, Inc.’s motion to defer determination of need. The filing asks that further action in furtherance of the PBRP be deferred so the Legislature can consider the Plan’s extraordinary costs and policy implications.²⁸
The Paxton filing reinforces, rather than replaces, the ALJs’ need findings. It identifies unresolved questions about the statutory basis and scope of the statewide 765-kV buildout and argues that the Legislature should have an opportunity to provide policy guidance.²⁸ The Legislature’s recent correspondence likewise requested additional time to reevaluate the 765-kV projects using updated generation and demand assumptions, including increased queued gas generation and potential market-design changes.³⁰ These developments reinforce the ALJs’ recommendation to deny the Applications on the existing record.
E. Routing
If the Commission does not adopt the recommendation to deny the Applications, the J27 Landowners take exception to the ALJs’ recommendation of Route 894. The PFD’s own balancing framework supports a two-step approach: first decide whether the Central Corridor’s State Park impacts should be avoided; if the Commission nevertheless selects that corridor, then compare Routes 487 and 894 across the full set of routing criteria.
The J27 Landowners respectfully submit that the Central Corridor should not be selected if another reasonable corridor can accommodate the Project with less impact to Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park. If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor, Route 487 is the better overall choice.
1. Route 894’s measured park advantage does not capture the full State Park impact nor eliminate the park problem.
Route 894 has no park or recreational area within 1,000 feet of its centerline and zero miles of right-of-way within the defined one-half-mile foreground visual zone, while Route 487 has one park within 1,000 feet and approximately 4.25 miles within that zone.⁹ The J27 Landowners concede that advantage. But the PFD expressly found that park impacts are not completely captured by the Environmental Assessment’s statistical information and that Route 894 would nevertheless be visible from many areas of both State Parks.¹⁰
The limitation is particularly important for a 765-kV project. The PFD finds that no 765-kV transmission line has been constructed in Texas and that the proposed structures would generally be 140 to 170 feet high, with a maximum anticipated height of 198 feet.¹¹ A one-half-mile metric developed for transmission-line routing should not be treated as the measure of the visual effect of structures of this scale from overlooks, roads, trails, and other sensitive viewing locations.
The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department evidence reinforces that point. The record identifies high-priority sensitive assets at Post Oak Ridge State Park and Colorado Bend State Park, including scenic overlooks and views associated with the Colorado River valley and iconic waterfalls, with recommended setback buffers extending well beyond one-half mile.¹² The qualitative impact therefore should not be treated as zero merely because Route 894 falls outside the one-half-mile metric.
The Central Corridor should therefore be avoided if a reasonable alternative can protect these resources better. The Commission’s decision in Docket No. 59315 is instructive: the Commission selected Route 559 after finding that it did not affect Dinosaur Valley State Park and adequately addressed the community value associated with the park.⁶ The record here likewise supports giving exceptional State Park resources meaningful weight rather than allowing a standard metric to decide the issue.
2. The Commission is not required to accept the marginal quantitative advantages of the Central Corridor
The Central Corridor should not be rejected merely because it does not win every routing metric. But neither should its incremental advantages be treated as controlling. The PFD recognizes that the Commission must balance competing routing factors and that every Focus Route has advantages and disadvantages.⁸
The Commission has previously made reasonable tradeoffs to avoid or reduce impacts to important community and park resources. The J27 Landowners do not contend that those prior decisions establish a mandatory preference for avoiding parks. Rather, they demonstrate that the Commission has previously recognized that a route’s higher cost, greater length, or other quantitative disadvantage does not necessarily outweigh significant impacts to unique protected or valued resources.¹⁴
The record therefore provides a reasonable alternative to the Central Corridor. Route CCG was shown to better protect the State Parks and other scenic and environmental resources while remaining within a relatively narrow cost range. Its estimated transmission-line cost is approximately $1.755 billion, roughly 4.4% above Route 894¹⁵ and can be a reasonable alternative to the state parks’ central corridor route impacts.
3. If the Commission selects the Central Corridor, Route 487 is superior to Route 894 on the overall balance of the record. Route 487 was independently selected by Commission Staff as its best overall routing option.²³
Route 487’s strongest advantage is infrastructure consolidation. The PFD found that Route 487 has the highest percentage of compatible-ROW paralleling among the Focus Routes.¹⁷ Route 487 has approximately 109.95 miles of compatible-ROW paralleling, or 49.64% of the route, compared with 98.02 miles, or 43.92%, for Route 894.²⁰ Route 487 also parallels approximately 22.05 miles of existing transmission lines, compared with only 5.66 miles for Route 894.²⁰ This materially greater paralleling concentrates infrastructure in existing corridors rather than creating additional standalone corridors and directly advances moderation of landowner impacts.
Route 487 also has modest but consistent advantages in cost and length. Staff’s evaluation and the PFD likewise recognize that Route 487’s estimated transmission-line cost is below Route 894’s.¹⁸–¹⁹ The Applicants’ Combined Data Table estimates Route 487’s transmission-line cost at approximately $1.665 billion, compared with approximately $1.681 billion for Route 894—a difference of approximately $16.1 million, or less than 1%.²⁰ Route 487 is also approximately 1.7 miles shorter than Route 894.²⁰ These differences are not independently dispositive, but they point in the same direction as the paralleling advantage.
Route 894’s habitable-structure advantage is narrower than the headline numbers suggest. The application data show 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of Route 894 and 96 for Route 487.²⁰ But the single-family-residence comparison is 80 for Route 894 versus 85 for Route 487—a difference of only five.²¹ The remaining difference in the broader structure count reflects other structure categories identified in the routing data. The J27 Landowners do not dispute the prudent-avoidance factor; they submit that it should not outweigh Route 487’s broader advantages.
The routing data also show several additional, though secondary, advantages for Route 487. The Applicants’ Combined Data Table shows 282 mapped stream crossings for Route 487 compared with 291 for Route 894; 0.07 miles of known habitat of federally listed endangered or threatened species compared with 0.09 miles; and 266.934 miles of areas of high archaeological/historical site potential compared with 278.115 miles.²⁰ Route 487 also has one private airstrip within 10,000 feet of its centerline compared with two for Route 894, two FAA-registered airports with a runway greater than 3,200 feet within 20,000 feet compared with three, and one FAA-registered airport without a runway greater than 3,200 feet within 10,000 feet compared with three.²⁰ These differences are not dispositive, particularly because Route 894 performs better on several other environmental and aviation measures, but they add to the cumulative comparison rather than detract from it.
The Colorado River and State Park impacts are the principal tradeoff for Route 487, but they do not make Route 894 superior overall. Route 487’s J11 crossing creates new transmission infrastructure across and ESSS-designated portion of the Colorado River and has significant park and viewshed effects. Route 894’s J22 crossing also creates new transmission infrastructure at the Colorado River and has its own park and viewshed impacts.²⁴ Route 894’s measured park advantage is therefore an advantage of degree, not the absence of impact. Once that advantage is appropriately weighted, Route 487’s materially greater paralleling and its cumulative advantages on the other routing measures support its selection.
The PFD’s own characterization of Route 894 makes the comparative weighting especially important. After comparing the Central Corridor alternatives, the ALJs stated that they were “tasked with choosing the least bad option” and recommended Route 894 “if any route must be chosen.”⁸ The J27 Landowners do not contend that this language demonstrates legal error by the ALJs. It does, however, underscore that Route 894 was not found to be affirmatively superior across the routing criteria. The Commission remains responsible for independently balancing the statutory factors, and the record supports giving meaningful weight to Route 487’s materially greater use of existing compatible corridors and its cumulative advantages.
4. Route 894 should not receive special weight simply because it was the Applicants’ “best meets” route
The Applicants’ “best meets” designation does not replace the Commission’s independent balancing. Applicants presented 122 routes, and the record establishes that all alternatives were technically feasible based on presently known conditions.²⁵ The Commission is therefore not being asked to substitute a speculative or landowner-generated route for an engineered alternative: Route 487 was one of the Applicants’ filed routes and was independently evaluated and selected by Commission Staff.²⁶
The Applicants’ park analysis also relies on standard quantitative metrics that the PFD found do not fully capture the visual effect on the State Parks.²⁷ The Commission should therefore evaluate the complete record rather than give the Applicants’ “best meets” route special weight.
IV. FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The J27 Landowners do not request a wholesale rewrite of the PFD’s Findings of Fact or Conclusions of Law. The requested relief is principally to adopt the ALJs’ denial recommendation and, if the Commission proceeds to routing, to modify the routing recommendation consistent with the record evidence discussed above.
The J27 Landowners specifically request that the Commission retain the PFD’s factual findings concerning the approximately 1,400 later-affected landowners who did not receive notice of a public meeting, while recognizing that the Commission has now rejected the PFD’s legal conclusion that Rule 22.52(a)(4) required another meeting. The factual history remains relevant to community input and the circumstances under which the final routing alternatives were developed.³¹
If the Commission adopts a Central Corridor route, the J27 Landowners request that the Commission’s final order explain, with reference to the evidence, why Route 894’s advantages in measured park proximity and habitable structures outweigh Route 487’s materially greater compatible-ROW paralleling, greater transmission-line paralleling, lower estimated cost, shorter length, avoidance of several strongly opposed links, additional advantages on secondary routing measures, and Staff’s independent recommendation of Route 487. The J27 Landowners respectfully request that the final order identify the relative weight assigned to these competing considerations so that the record reflects a consistent application of the routing criteria.³²
V. CONCLUSION
The J27 Landowners respectfully request that the Commission adopt the ALJs’ recommendation to deny the Applications because Applicants failed to establish need. The J27 Landowners recognize that the Commission’s August 28, 2026 order in Docket No. 59315 has resolved the public-meeting legal issue differently from the PFD. The J27 Landowners therefore do not rely on notice as an independent basis for denial.
If the Applications proceed, the Central Corridor should be avoided if a reasonable alternative can better protect the State Parks. The PFD’s qualitative findings demonstrate that the standard one-half-mile park metric does not capture the full visual effect of a 765-kV line, and Route 894 itself would remain visible from portions of both parks.  The Commission has precedent choosing routes which protected State Parks.
If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor, Route 487 should be selected over Route 894. Route 894 has real advantages, especially on the measured park and habitable-structure metrics. But those advantages do not outweigh Route 487’s substantially greater use of existing compatible corridors and transmission-line paralleling, shorter length, lower estimated cost, nine fewer mapped stream crossings, lower archaeological/historical-potential mileage, lower measured mileage of known federally listed habitat, fewer nearby private airstrips and FAA-registered airports on the applicable measures, avoidance of heavily opposed links, and Staff’s independent selection of Route 487 as the best overall routing option.
For these reasons, the J27 Landowners respectfully request that the Commission deny the Applications. Alternatively, if the Commission determines that the Project should proceed, the Commission should select a non-Central-Corridor alternative such as Route CCG. If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor, the Commission should select Route 487.
CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE
I certify that a true and correct copy of the foregoing instrument has been served on all parties of record on this 2nd day of September 2026.

/s/ Paul Grimme
Paul Grimme

comparison is 80 for Route 894 versus 85 for Route 487-a difference of only
five.21 The remaining difference in the broader structure count reflects other
structure categories identified in the routing data. The J27 Landowners do not
dispute the prudent-avoidance factor; they submit that it should not outweigh
Route 487's broader advantages.
The routing data also show several additional, though secondary, advantages
for Route 487. The Applicants' Combined Data Table shows 282 mapped stream
crossings for Route 487 compared with 291 for Route 894; 0.07 miles of known
habitat of federally listed endangered or threatened species compared with 0.09
miles; and 266.934 miles of areas of high archaeological/historical site potential
compared with 278.115 miles.2° Route 487 also has one private airstrip within
10,000 feet of its centerline compared with two for Route 894, two FAA-registered
airports with a runway greater than 3,200 feet within 20,000 feet compared with
three, and one FAA-registered airport without a runway greater than 3,200 feet
within 10,000 feet compared with three.2° These differences are not dispositive,
particularly because Route 894 performs better on several other environmental and


                                          8
 aviation measures, but they add to the cumulative comparison rather than detract
from it.
The Colorado River and State Park impacts are the principal tradeoff for
Route 487, but they do not make Route 894 superior overall. Route 487's Jll
crossing creates new transmission infrastructure across and ESSS-designated
portion of the Colorado River and has significant park and viewshed effects. Route
894's J22 crossing also creates new transmission infrastructure at the Colorado
River and has its own park and viewshed impacts.24 Route 894's measured park
advantage is therefore an advantage of degree, not the absence of impact. Once that
advantage is appropriately weighted, Route 487's materially greater paralleling and
its cumulative advantages on the other routing measures support its selection.
The PFD's own characterization of Route 894 makes the comparative
weighting especially important. After comparing the Central Corridor
alternatives, the ALJs stated that they were "tasked with choosing the least bad
option" and recommended Route 894 "if any route must be chosen.°'8 The J27
Landowners do not contend that this language demonstrates legal error by the
ALJs. It does, however, underscore that Route 894 was not found to be
affirmatively superior across the routing criteria. The Commission remains
responsible for independently balancing the statutory factors, and the record
supports giving meaningful weight to Route 487's materially greater use of
existing compatible corridors and its cumulative advantages.

4. Route 894 should not receive special weight simply because it was the
Applicants , " best meets" route

The Applicants' "best meets" designation does not replace the Commission's
independent balancing. Applicants presented 122 routes, and the record establishes
that all alternatives were technically feasible based on presently known


                                         9
 conditions.25 The Commission is therefore not being asked to substitute a
speculative or landowner-generated route for an engineered alternative: Route 487
was one of the Applicants' filed routes and was independently evaluated and
selected by Commission Staff.26
The Applicants' park analysis also relies on standard quantitative metrics that the
PFD found do not fully capture the visual effect on the State Parks.27 The
Commission should therefore evaluate the complete record rather than give the
Applicants' "best meets" route special weight.

IV. FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

The J27 Landowners do not request a wholesale rewrite of the PFD' s Findings of
Fact or Conclusions of Law. The requested relief is principally to adopt the ALJs'
denial recommendation and, if the Commission proceeds to routing, to modify the
routing recommendation consistent with the record evidence discussed above.
The J27 Landowners specifically request that the Commission retain the PFD' s
factual findings concerning the approximately 1,400 later-affected landowners who
did not receive notice of a public meeting, while recognizing that the Commission
has now rejected the PFD' s legal conclusion that Rule 22.52(a)(4) required another
meeting. The factual history remains relevant to community input and the
circumstances under which the final routing alternatives were developed.31
If the Commission adopts a Central Corridor route, the J27 Landowners request
that the Commission's final order explain, with reference to the evidence, why
Route 894's advantages in measured park proximity and habitable structures
outweigh Route 487's materially greater compatible-ROW paralleling, greater
transmission-line paralleling, lower estimated cost, shorter length, avoidance of
several strongly opposed links, additional advantages on secondary routing
measures, and Staff' s independent recommendation of Route 487. The J27


                                         10
 Landowners respectfully request that the final order identify the relative weight
assigned to these competing considerations so that the record reflects a consistent
application of the routing criteria.32

V. CONCLUSION

The J27 Landowners respectfully request that the Commission adopt the
ALJs' recommendation to deny the Applications because Applicants failed to
establish need. The J27 Landowners recognize that the Commission's August 28,
2026 order in Docket No. 59315 has resolved the public-meeting legal issue
differently from the PFD. The J27 Landowners therefore do not rely on notice as
an independent basis for denial.
If the Applications proceed, the Central Corridor should be avoided if a
reasonable alternative can better protect the State Parks. The PFD' s qualitative
findings demonstrate that the standard one-half-mile park metric does not capture
the full visual effect of a 765-kV line, and Route 894 itself would remain visible
from portions of both parks. The Commission has precedent choosing routes
which protected State Parks.
If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor, Route 487 should
be selected over Route 894. Route 894 has real advantages, especially on the
measured park and habitable-structure metrics. But those advantages do not
outweigh Route 487's substantially greater use of existing compatible corridors
and transmission-line paralleling, shorter length, lower estimated cost, nine fewer
mapped stream crossings, lower archaeological/historical-potential mileage, lower
measured mileage of known federally listed habitat, fewer nearby private airstrips
and FAA-registered airports on the applicable measures, avoidance of heavily
opposed links, and Staff' s independent selection of Route 487 as the best overall
routing option.


                                         11
 For these reasons, the J27 Landowners respectfully request that the Commission
deny the Applications. Alternatively, if the Commission determines that the Project
should proceed, the Commission should select a non-Central-Corridor alternative
such as Route CCG. If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor,
the Commission should select Route 487.
